title: How much money is in the world?
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore how much money exists in the world, starting with US dollars in circulation. They explain the Federal Reserve's money supply measures M0, M1, and M2 (M3 was dropped in 2006), using the July 2013 figures, and note that roughly half to two-thirds of US cash is held overseas. They discuss why tracking global money is hard without a central bank in every country, using Zimbabwe's hyperinflation and its abandoned Zim dollar as the main example. They then cover the idea of a universal world currency: historical precedents, pros and cons, Keynes's proposal, regional currency unions (West and Central African CFA franc, Euro, the proposed North American "amero"), and the closing listener mail segment.
topics: how much money is in the world

segments.title: Opening banter and the thirty-eight hundred dollar question
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open by asking how much cash they carry and explain that dividing the world's US dollars among Americans comes to about $3,800 each.

segments.title: M0 money supply and US dollars worldwide
segments.summary: They define the M0 money supply as all bills and coins in circulation, cite about $1.2 trillion as of July 2013, and note that roughly half to two-thirds is held overseas.

segments.title: M1 and M2 money supply measures
segments.summary: They explain M1 adds checking and travelers checks, and M2 adds savings, money market funds, and small CDs, about $10.5 trillion in mid-2013. They say M3 was dropped in 2006.

segments.title: Tracking money and Zimbabwe's hyperinflation
segments.summary: They explain the Fed tracks money it prints, while countries without central banks make global tallies hard. Zimbabwe's money printing led to hyperinflation, with prices doubling roughly every day and a Zim dollar note later sold on eBay.

segments.title: Zimbabwe's currency abandonment and the 2008 estimate
segments.summary: They describe Zimbabwe's annual inflation estimates, the 2009 switch to foreign currencies such as the South African rand and US dollar, and the lack of a buyback program.

segments.title: Estimating global money supply from Steve Hanke's blog
segments.summary: Chuck reports that an economist's blog tracking 135 currencies in 167 countries last gave figures for December 2010, with M0 about $5 trillion and M2 about $55 trillion.

segments.title: Universal world currency: history, pros and cons
segments.summary: They discuss Keynes's proposal, the historical Roman and Chinese currencies, and the post-World War II attempt. Pros include no conversion fees and no speculation against a single currency. Cons include the gold standard debate, who would run it, and losing the ability to devalue a currency to fix a sluggish economy.
topics: pros and cons of a single currency

segments.title: Regional currency unions and the amero
segments.summary: They cover the West and Central African CFA francs, the euro, failed Central and South American plans, and the North American Union with its proposed amero.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh read listener mail, including books, postcards, music, and vinyl sent in by listeners, then sign off with contact information.
